aiOverview.content: View all A cassette tape consists of a magnetic, iron-oxide coated polyester film housed within a plastic shell, featuring two spools (supply and take-up) that move the tape across a record/playback head. Key components include felt pressure pads for head contact, slip sheets to reduce friction, guide rollers for alignment, and write-protection tabs. This video shows the inner workings of a cassette tape:1mGary Keep IT SimpleYouTube• Oct 7, 2025 1m Plastic Shell/Casing: The protective outer housing, typically made of two halves screwed or welded together. Magnetic Tape: A thin, iron-oxide or chromium dioxide-coated polyester film that stores audio signals in four tracks (two per side). Spools/Reels (Supply & Take-up): Two geared wheels that hold the tape and move it from side to side. Leader Tape: Non-magnetic plastic tape at the beginning and end of the magnetic tape to strengthen it and allow for smooth transitions during auto-reverse. Pressure Pad: A small piece of felt, often supported by a metal spring, that pushes the magnetic tape against the recorder’s playback/record head. Guide Rollers: Small rollers or plastic pillars located at the corners to ensure the tape runs in a straight, accurate path. Slip Sheets (Liners): Low-friction plastic sheets inside the shell that allow the tape pancakes to spin smoothly. Write-Protect Tabs: Small plastic tabs on the top edge that, when removed, prevent accidental recording or erasure. Capstan Hole: An opening for the tape deck's capstan (spinning shaft) and pinch roller to pull the tape at a constant speed. Note: The magnetic tape is usually around 0.150.150.15 inches (3.813.813.81 mm) wide, often referred to as 1/8-inch tape.
